analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 100% income tax on bonuses paid by big bailed-out banks, funding housing programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew only two cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed a 100% additional income tax on bonuses paid to current and former employees of firms that received more than $5 billion in bailout capital under the 2008 financial rescue, plus the mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Employees could avoid the tax by returning or waiving their bonus, and firms that repaid their bailout money in full were exempt. All revenue raised would have gone to the Department of Housing and Urban Development to fund community development and mortgage-relief programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and struggling homeowners. Executives of bailed-out firms earning over $250,000 would owe the full amount of their bailout-era bonuses back to the government, and the money would flow to HUD community development and mortgage-relief programs rather than to Wall Street pay packages.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 100% additional tax on bonus, retention, and incentive payments from firms that received more than $5 billion in TARP capital infusions, and from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac [S2][S3].
Exempts employees who irrevocably waive or return their bonus, and exempts firms that repaid bailout funds so that less than $5 billion remains outstanding [S2][S3].
Deposits all revenue raised into Department of Housing and Urban Development accounts to fund community development programs, which the bill's title says were meant for mortgage workouts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Current and former employees of large bailed-out financial firms who earned more than $250,000 in a year and kept their bailout-era bonuses; they would owe the federal government up to the full amount of those bonuses. The firms themselves would face pressure to restructure or withhold incentive pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives of bailed-out Wall Street firms

drawbacks.text: The tax is keyed to adjusted gross income above $250,000, not to the bonus alone, so an affected employee could owe 100% tax on income up to the size of the bonus even beyond the bonus payment itself [S3].
The exemption for firms that repaid their bailout funds means executives at banks that returned TARP money quickly would face no clawback, limiting the tax to a shrinking set of recipients [S2][S3].

The tax applies to bonus payments received after December 31, 2008, reaching payments made before the bill was introduced, and retroactive taxes on already-paid compensation drew good-faith fairness and legal objections when similar measures were proposed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people outside the affected firms, the cost is essentially zero and the benefit is direct: bailout-era bonuses are clawed back and the proceeds fund housing and mortgage-relief programs. The main honest objections are that the tax reaches beyond the bonus itself to all income above $250,000 for affected employees, that repaid-bailout firms escape entirely, and that retroactive taxation of past compensation raises fairness concerns. On balance the design flaws narrow the bill's reach without changing its basic direction: it takes from bailed-out executives and gives to housing programs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up; it died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on July 31, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services Committee [S1][S5].
Two House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded in the bill's action history after the initial referral; the last action listed is the referral itself [S5].
The bill never received a vote in either chamber and expired when the 111th Congress ended [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and employees of the large banks and mortgage-finance firms that received over $5 billion in bailout capital kept their bonuses untaxed, and the bailed-out financial industry avoided any bonus clawback. Community development and mortgage-relief programs never received the revenue the bill would have directed to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bailee-out bank executives kept their bonuses

for.name: Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Recoupment of Wall Street Bonus Act and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 2 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other member of either party did.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred; no action was ever recorded.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support came from three Democrats (the sponsor plus two cosponsors) out of 253 House Democrats; no Republican supported it, and the committee chairs whose panels held the bill were Democrats, so the bill lacked support even within its own majority party.

industries.industry: Bailed-out Wall Street financial firms and their executives
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 100% tax on bonuses, retention pay, and incentive payments at firms still holding more than $5 billion in bailout capital, clawing back executive pay that had been paid while taxpayers were covering the firms' losses. Firms that repaid their bailout money were exempt, so the burden fell on those most dependent on public support.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac employees
industries.note: The two mortgage-finance giants, which had been placed under federal conservatorship, were explicitly covered, so their high-earning employees would have owed the full bonus tax.

industries.industry: Community development and housing counseling organizations
industries.note: All revenue from the bonus tax would have been deposited at HUD to fund community development programs, including mortgage-relief efforts, providing a new funding stream for housing assistance.
